title: My Own Mayday
blurb: The first distress call comes in your own voice, from a ship in trouble you have never been in. The next is dated three weeks ahead, names a nav beacon you have never visited, and warns of pirates waiting there. They are. Each call after it names another place and another date, always a little ahead of you, and something out in the dark has started listening to them too. Stop following, and whoever made the first call stays unanswered, and what is listening in the dark follows the route to its last date without you. Who sent them, and what is waiting at the last date?
inYourWords: I have a Sidewinder still in yard paint, a few hundred credits, and nobody to talk to but the ship. The only other voice I hear is Teague's, the dock hand at my first station, and he only ever sends messages. Then a mayday came in on a band nothing uses. The voice was mine. I have played it back a dozen times, and it is my voice, down to the way I say please. I never sent it, and I have never been in the trouble it describes.
beacon: Every call rides the carrier of a Guardian beacon. If a beacon is sending my voice, the beacon is where I find out how.

title: Black Box
blurb: The yard sold you the cheapest Sidewinder on the lot and missed the flight recorder. Its last pilot, Ines Harrow, went missing eleven months ago, and a well-dressed man named Selden Pryce will pay you on delivery to find out why. Every lead takes you further along her last route: a salvage field, a scrap yard, a distress call nobody answered. Every report you send, he reads very carefully. Get it wrong, and whatever happened to her is buried for good, along with anyone who helped you look. What did Ines Harrow find out there?
inYourWords: I bought the cheapest Sidewinder on the lot, with a clean title and a few hundred credits left over. The yard said it was wiped by the book. They missed the flight recorder. Every time I start the drive it plays the same four seconds: a woman's voice, calm, reading out a set of coordinates and her name. Ines Harrow. Nobody has seen her in eleven months.
beacon: The coordinates on the recorder are a Guardian beacon. It was the last place Ines Harrow logged before she went quiet, and the first place anyone looking for her would go.

title: The Far Side
tone: Aching long-distance friendship, wry and tender
blurb: Nico Sandoval answered your post on the jobs board with a terrible joke and a good offer: split the contracts, you fly the cargo in, Nico flies it out. A year of shared jobs and late-night messages makes Nico the best friend you have out here. You have never seen Nico's face. Every message arrives nine hours after it was sent, and Nico describes stars you cannot find on any chart. Miss what Nico is not saying, and you lose the one person out here who has always been on your side. Where is Nico, really?
inYourWords: Nobody lends a Sidewinder pilot anything, not even company, so I posted on the jobs board for a partner. One reply came. Nico. Bad jokes, good maths, and a ship Nico will not describe. We split the work: I fly the cargo in and Nico flies it out. We have not met yet. We keep just missing each other.
beacon: Nico's messages reach me stamped with the routing code of a Guardian beacon, and they arrive full of crackle. Nico says a data-link scan of the beacon will clear the line. I would like to hear Nico properly.

title: Journeyman
tone: Hopeful guild quest, warm and wry
blurb: The Companions of the Lane are older than the Pilots Federation, and their mark still opens doors a licence does not. To earn it you walk the Circuit: nine old masters scattered across the bubble, one for each craft a pilot can learn, and none of them marks your book until the work is good. Mother Agathe, who keeps the last open guild house, swears a strongbox opens for whoever brings a full book home. Linus, the only other journeyman on the road, is always one master ahead of you, with far too much money. The masters are old, and if nobody finishes, the guild dies with them. Why has no house sent a journeyman in twenty years?
inYourWords: I had a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits, and nowhere to sleep but the cockpit when I found the guild house: a common room, a row of empty bunks, and a board of names with most of them crossed out. Mother Agathe keeps it. She feeds anyone who works. She watched me work for a week, then put a book in my hands: a page for a Guardian beacon, a page for each of nine masters, and one for a masterwork. She says a strongbox opens for whoever fills it. I wrote my name inside the cover.
beacon: The first page of the book belongs to no master. It asks for the data from a Guardian beacon, the oldest machine anyone has found that still does its job. Mother Agathe says every journeyman starts there, to see how long good work outlasts the people who did it.

title: Good Standing
blurb: You have flown alone for years. Then Maren Holt watched you hold a line in a conflict zone after your wing ran, and sponsored you into the Brightwater Mutual: four hundred independent pilots, one share each, a fund for the bad weeks, and a wing that comes when you call. Augustin Pell, the last of its founders, says the charter is one line long: the Mutual looks after its own. The pay is the best you have had, and the wars keep getting bigger, every one of them through a broker the council will not discuss. If the Mutual loses its way, four hundred pilots lose the only home some of them have, and the friends who brought you in pay first. Who chooses the Mutual's wars?
inYourWords: I have flown independent for six years. I have a ship I trust, some engineering done on it, and enough savings that one bad week would not finish me, though two might. Last month I held a line in a conflict zone after my wing ran, and the pilot who came back for me was Maren Holt of the Brightwater Mutual. She has offered to sponsor me. Four hundred pilots, one share each, a fund for the bad weeks, and a wing on call. Augustin Pell, who founded it, bought me a drink and told me the charter is one line. I have never belonged to anything. I have not said yes yet.
beacon: Every member of the Mutual flies the Founding Run before their first vote: a data-link scan of a Guardian beacon, as the founding twelve did the night they signed the charter. Maren says it is the only test the Mutual sets.

title: The Omphalos
blurb: You have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and more credits than you will ever spend. Then Hester Vane comes aboard: ninety years old, sixty of them spent hunting Raxxla, and the last living member of the Dark Wheel. She needs your carrier and a year, because the only real lead the Wheel ever had is a Guardian star chart a million years old, and reading it takes the whole width of the galaxy. A salvage magnate with carriers of his own has heard about the chart, and he has never lost an auction. Read it wrong, and Raxxla goes to a man who strips Guardian sites for collectors, and Hester's sixty years end with nothing. Is Raxxla on the chart at all?
inYourWords: I own a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships I rarely fly, and more credits than I can spend. Not much surprises me any more. Then an old explorer named Hester Vane docked at my carrier, asked for tea, and told me she was the last of the Dark Wheel. She has been looking for Raxxla for sixty years. She did not ask for money. She asked for my carrier, and for a year.
beacon: Hester says every Guardian beacon's data-link carries the same star chart, and that every member of the Dark Wheel scanned one and came away with something they could not read. She thinks it lists a world no human catalogue does. To read it, I need something aboard that reads Guardian charts, and she says the beacon is where I will find that too.

title: The Scholarship
blurb: You grew up in your parents' scrapyard, and the only person there who was kind to you was the engineer they hired, who helped you build a Sidewinder from scrap and fitted a transponder nobody can follow. You ran. Months later, half-starved at the edge of the charts, Augustin Rell offers you a scholarship: training, combat certification, steady contracts, and a vitamin shot to put the weight back on. Since that shot you have not lost a fight, or backed away from one. Every contract is a rescue, Rell says, and every target deserves it. If he is wrong, you are the weapon, and the engineer who saved you is not safe either. What was in the shot?
inYourWords: I grew up in my parents' scrapyard, mostly in the way. The engineer they hired was the only one who ever asked whether I had eaten. The engineer helped me put a Sidewinder together out of three wrecks and fitted a transponder my parents can't follow. I left one night and didn't look back. That was months ago. I have the Sidewinder, a few hundred credits, and nobody who knows where I am.
beacon: The scholarship's first contract after certification: fly to a Guardian beacon, make a data-link scan, and bring the Lantern Fund everything it holds. Rell says the Fund collects them. The fee would feed me for a year.

title: The Hillside
blurb: Three hundred and forty miners live at Ukah Mining Territory, on a grey moon in LHS 145, and they have seventy-two hours. The Kade Combine has ringed their system with interdictors: leave the mine, or be there when the settlement's shield fails. Their foreman, Tamsin Rook, flew on your wing for six years and never asked you for anything. She still has not asked. You have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and three days, and Varro Kade has never lost a siege. From the moment your carrier arrives, he stops caring about the mine. If the shield falls, so does every family on that hillside. What is Kade after now?
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, more ships than I can fly in a month, and enough credits that nobody has been able to threaten me in years. Tamsin Rook flew on my wing for six years, then went off to dig rock on a moon in LHS 145 that nobody has heard of. Last night she called. The Kade Combine has blockaded her system, and her settlement's shield has three days of power left. She did not ask me to come. She said she only needed someone to know. I have already plotted the jump.
beacon: Rook says the Combine's trouble started far past the edge of the bubble, at a Guardian beacon where Kade has kept a ship parked for a year, listening. Before I go to her, I am going to scan that beacon and find out what he is listening for.

title: One Star
tone: Comic sightseeing farce, dry and warm
blurb: Horace Penhallow is the most feared critic in human space: one line in Penhallow's Starlanes once emptied a starport bar that had served drinks for two hundred years. Now he has booked a week aboard your fleet carrier for a new edition, with his own itinerary of ten sights, starting at a Guardian beacon. Wynn Odoro, who runs your carrier's bar, says one star will empty it for a decade. You have flown through wars without blinking, and you have never been reviewed. Penhallow writes everything down, including you, and has not smiled once. Get it wrong, and Wynn's bar and everyone who drinks there pay for it. What is he really writing in that notebook?
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and more credits than I can spend, and I have not taken a day off in years. There is always a jump to plot or a market to restock. Yesterday Wynn Odoro, who runs the bar on my carrier, came up to the bridge white as a sheet. Horace Penhallow has booked passage. The Horace Penhallow. He wants a week, a cabin with a view, and a tour of ten sights. Wynn says he reviews everything, the host included. I said I would fly him round for a week. How hard can it be?
beacon: Sight one on Penhallow's itinerary is a Guardian beacon, scanned by data-link with him watching from the jump seat. He says a review that starts anywhere else is a press release.

title: Runner-Up
blurb: For twenty years you have come second to Delphine Ashcroft: in trade, at the edge of the Formidine Rift, and by a few minutes at the first data-link with the Guardian beacon in Synuefe KU-F b44-4, as the plaque at Lave Station still says. Now she is retiring, and she has called you to Lave for one last contest on the old terms: eleven days, three legs, and the loser says it out loud on the Lanes Report. First she asked you to fly back to that beacon and scan it again. Lose, and the record stands for good, and so does the last word between you. Why did she send you back to the beacon?
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of engineered ships and more credits than I will ever spend, and there is one name I have never beaten. Delphine Ashcroft and I have raced each other for twenty years, and she has won every time, including the race that matters most to me: the first data-link with the Guardian beacon in Synuefe KU-F b44-4. Her name is on the plaque at Lave Station. Mine is under it. I have not been back to that beacon since. Last week she told me she is retiring, and challenged me to one more contest before she goes. I said yes before she finished the sentence.
beacon: Ashcroft asked me to go back to the beacon in Synuefe KU-F b44-4, where she beat me twenty years ago, and scan it again before I come to Lave Station. I have scanned it. Something happened that did not happen the first time.

title: The Milk Run
tone: Elegiac family drama, quiet and wry
blurb: For fifty years Ida Vance has flown the same five stops in LHS 2270: one refinery and four farms in a system nobody visits. You left at seventeen and became a pilot the whole bubble knows, and you have spoken to her ten times since. Now her heart is failing and she has a month. She has asked for one last run with you, and one detour first: the Guardian beacon where your father died before you were born. Your brother Tobias has not forgiven you, and your mother keeps a paper ledger she will not let anyone read. Miss this month, and you never learn what she has been carrying, or make your peace with the people she carried it for. What is in the ledger?
inYourWords: I left home at seventeen in a Sidewinder and did not look back. My mother, Ida, has flown the same five stops in LHS 2270 for fifty years: one refinery and four farms, the same faces every week, small cargo and smaller money. I needed more than that, and I got it: a fleet carrier, a hangar of engineered ships, and a name people know. We have spoken perhaps ten times in twenty years. Last night she sent word that her heart is failing and she has a month, and she asked me to fly the run with her one last time. My brother Tobias, who stayed, sent nothing.
beacon: My father, Cal Vance, died beside a Guardian beacon out past the edge of the bubble, a month before I was born. My mother has never seen the place. Before the run she has asked me to fly her there, and I am going to scan the beacon while she watches.

title: The Long Hour
blurb: Two years after the Thargoid war, the Joint Remembrance Board is giving you its highest citation, for the Long Hour, when an evacuation pilot held a lane open through a Thargoid swarm and eleven thousand people reached the jump point. In three months Commodore Lucan Strade will present it himself. You do not remember the hour: twelve minutes without air in a breached cockpit took all of it, and your flight recorder came back blank. Rhea Calder flew on your wing that day, and she has one thing to say about the citation: don't take it. Accept the wrong record, and the truth of the hour, and everyone who paid for it, is buried under your name. What happened in the lane?
inYourWords: I flew evacuations through the whole war on a wing of three, callsign Ladder: Rhea Calder, Ansel Teague and me. Ansel didn't come home. Since the peace I've built up a fleet carrier, more ships than I can fly and more credits than I need, and mostly I haul cargo nobody is shooting at. Now the Remembrance Board says I held the lane at the Long Hour and saved eleven thousand people. I'd like to believe it. I don't remember a minute of it.
beacon: The citation says my hour was reconstructed from outside telemetry. An old anti-xeno hand at Veterans Retreat told me what that means: all through the war, the Guardian beacons were listening for Thargoids, and the Board pulled its record from them. If a beacon heard my hour, I'm going to hear it too.

title: Standing Order
blurb: You parked your fleet carrier over a mining outpost for a week's refit, and that afternoon you cleared its raiders before your coffee went cold. Ada Corwen, who has run the outpost for thirty years, asked you to stay a little longer. So you stay. Your ships fly the patrols, your carrier's market buys the ore, and the outpost has never been safer, or needed you more. Then Rennick Hale, who buys mining claims for a living, docks, looks up at your carrier, and asks how long you mean to stay. Get it wrong, and the outpost Ada held together for thirty years is sold out from under her. What does Hale know about this place that Ada will not say?
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships engineered as far as they go, and more credits than I will ever spend. Nobody has needed anything from me in years except a docking fee. Last week I parked the carrier over a mining outpost on the edge of the bubble for a refit, and that afternoon raiders came for the outpost's ore. I dealt with them before my coffee went cold. Ada Corwen, who runs the place, threw me a party in the ore hall and asked me to stay a little longer. I said a week. The week is up, and I have not plotted a jump.
beacon: The outpost's founders came out here thirty years ago following the signal of a Guardian beacon, and every pilot the outpost counts as its own has flown to a beacon and made a data-link scan of it. Ada has asked me to. Nobody has asked me to belong anywhere in a long time.

title: Next of Kin
tone: Protective found-family chase, warm and watchful
blurb: For twenty years Vesna Kaul beat you to every contract worth having. Now she is dead, her ship lost on a quiet run, and her will names you guardian of a daughter you never knew she had. Linnet is fourteen, furious, and a better natural pilot than anyone on your carrier. She hums in her sleep, the same few notes every night. Dr. Corin Wexley, the soft-spoken scientist who paid for her mother's last survey, has asked to meet her, and Vesna's will has one more line, underlined twice: never let him. Fail, and Linnet goes to the one man her mother told you to keep her from. What does he need from a fourteen-year-old girl?
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and more credits than I will ever spend. For twenty years there was one pilot I could never beat, Vesna Kaul, and I think she was half the reason I kept flying. Last week a Pilots Federation clerk told me she was dead, and that her will names me guardian of her daughter. I did not know she had one. Linnet came aboard this morning with one bag, walked past me without a word, and chose the cabin furthest from mine. The carrier has never been this quiet.
beacon: Linnet hums the same few notes in her sleep, and has all her life. The carrier's comms log matches them to the carrier signal of a Guardian beacon. She has never seen one, and for the first time since she came aboard, she has asked me for something.

title: Honest Work
blurb: You are a good pilot and better company, and you have not told the whole truth in years. For sixteen years Bram Tolliver, eighty next month and the proudest old man at Hutton Orbital, has believed his child is a lieutenant in the Federal Navy, because that is what your letters say. For his birthday he asks for one thing: a picture of his lieutenant beside a lit Guardian beacon. You scan the beacon so it lights for the camera, and what comes aboard with the scan cannot abide a false record. From then on every message your ship sends goes out with a correction attached. If the truth reaches Bram the wrong way, it costs him his pride in front of everyone he knows, and costs you your father. Can you tell him before your ship does?
inYourWords: I fly freight and the odd charter in a ship I have put real money into, engineering and all, and I have enough saved that a bad month would not sink me. I am good at the work and better at the talking. When a cargo is late, it was pirates. When my sister Hanne asks, I visit Dad often. My father, Bram, flew Eagles off a Federal Navy carrier for thirty years, and I applied to the Navy flight academy because of him. I washed out at nineteen. I never told him. I wrote to him as a lieutenant instead, and I have been writing ever since. He turns eighty next month at Hutton Orbital, and he has asked for a picture of me at a Guardian beacon, because my last letter said I was posted to a Navy survey of Guardian sites. I am going to get him one.
beacon: My letters say I am posted to a Navy survey of Guardian sites. For his eightieth birthday my father has asked for a picture of his lieutenant beside a Guardian beacon, lit up. A beacon only lights for a data-link scan, so I am going to scan one and take the picture.

title: Dark Horse
blurb: Every pilot at Ray Gateway knows your name, and none of them takes you seriously. You are the one at the end of the bar who says the Guardian beacons answer back. While you were out scanning one to settle Moss Varley's bet, somebody put your name on the ballot for Pilots' Steward, the seat that sets the docking levy and runs the rescue fund. Imogen Thale has held it for fourteen years. The vote is in eleven days, the station newsfeed calls you the joke candidate, and Moss has already had the badges made. Laugh it off, and the rescue fund every pilot pays into stays in the hands that hold it now. Who filed your name, and why?
inYourWords: I fly a working ship out of Ray Gateway in Diaguandri. I have done some engineering on it, I have savings enough for a bad month, and I have a seat at the end of the pilots' bar that everybody knows is mine. I also have a theory: that the Guardian beacons answer back if you scan them properly. Nobody at the bar believes it. Last month Moss Varley opened a book on it at eleven to one, and I flew out to settle the matter. On the way home the newsfeed told me my name is on the ballot for Pilots' Steward, against Imogen Thale, who has held the seat for fourteen years. I did not put it there. Moss says he has no idea who did, and he has already had badges made.
beacon: Moss Varley opened a book at the bar on whether a Guardian beacon answers back when it is scanned properly, at eleven to one against. I flew out to the beacon to settle it, and I have scanned it. I am not saying yet who won the book.

title: Point of Order
blurb: The Ice is two frozen worlds at the edge of Eranin: four thousand miners and one seat on the Eranin Assembly. You filed for it against the Speaker's nephew in a bar, on a bet, with a platform one line long, and won by eleven votes. You have never read a law, you live in your cockpit, and Dee Mwangi, the refinery foreman, has called you a joke to your face. Speaker Barnaby Quell welcomes you warmly and puts you on a committee that has not met in forty years. Perpetua Gilchrist, Clerk of the Assembly for forty-one years, hands you the rules, all eleven hundred of them. Lose your nerve, and four thousand people lose their say over their own worlds. Why is the Speaker so pleased to see you?
inYourWords: I have a working ship, some engineering done and savings that one bad month could take. I haul ore for the miners on the Ice, out at the edge of Eranin, and every time I dock I watch the Assembly's freight levy come off their pay. When the Ice's seat came up, the only candidate was the Speaker's nephew. I filed against him in a bar in Azeban City, on a bet, with one line: scrap the levy. I won by eleven votes. I am now the Member for the Ice. I have never read a law in my life, and I have just been handed eleven hundred of them.
beacon: Speaker Quell put me on the Committee on Xeno-Antiquities. It has not met in forty years and has one item outstanding: a survey of a Guardian beacon that the Assembly paid for and never received. The Clerk says a member who sits on a committee does its work. So I am going to fly out and scan it.

title: Blind Charter
tone: Tense amnesia thriller, wry and kind
blurb: You wake in your own cockpit at a starport you do not remember reaching, with nine hours missing. Your log says you flew a blind charter for no fee, scanned a Guardian beacon, then paid a privacy clinic to take the memory out of your head. A message in your own voice is waiting, locked for one day. At the foot of your boarding ramp stands Anselm Coyle, an Imperial contract recovery agent with beautiful manners, who would like to know where you took her. You have no idea who she is. Give Coyle what he asks for, and whoever she is loses whatever she was running toward. Why did you agree to forget?
inYourWords: I fly a working ship with some engineering on it, and I have saved enough that I can turn down a job I do not like. I haul, I run charters, and for years I have turned down the blind ones, where the client stays sealed and you sign to have the job taken out of your memory afterwards. Yesterday, apparently, I said yes to one. I woke an hour ago with nine hours gone, a clinic receipt with my own thumbprint on it, and a polite man at the foot of my ramp asking questions I cannot answer. I do not know what I did. I would very much like to know why I did it.
beacon: I do not remember scanning it. The cockpit recorder kept four minutes of the nine hours: me flying out past the edge of the bubble to a Guardian beacon as if I knew exactly why, and running the data-link without a second's pause. The clinic holds the rest, sealed, with the memory.

title: The Right Seat
tone: Fragile comeback story, quiet and wry
blurb: Fourteen months ago a drive fault dropped your ship out of supercruise beside the rings of Uszaa 2 with eight sightseers aboard. Ice cracked the canopy, everyone lived, and the inquiry cleared you. It also recorded that you were off your plotted course, and nobody, you included, can say why. You have not carried a passenger since. Now Tilly Marsh, who was fourteen and in the front row that day, has started at Agnes Rowntree's flight school and asked for you in the right seat for her training hours. Her father has told you to stay away from her. Turn her down, and a girl who means to fly loses her instructor, and you lose your last reason to fly with anyone again. Why did you turn off the course?
inYourWords: I have a ship that works, some engineering done on it and savings enough for a bad month, and for fourteen months I have flown the same short route through the Lave cluster with the passenger cabin full of crates. I used to fly charters. Then a drive fault dropped me out of supercruise beside the rings of Uszaa 2 with eight people aboard. Everyone lived, and the inquiry cleared me. It also says I was off my plotted course, and I hit my head on the way out of the ring, and I do not remember why I turned. Agnes Rowntree taught me to fly twenty years ago. She says I can haul crates for the rest of my life, or I can come and sit in the right seat for a girl who was on that charter and still means to be a pilot.
beacon: Every cadet at Agnes Rowntree's flight school flies one long solo before their licence: out past the edge of the bubble to a Guardian beacon, a data-link scan, and home. I flew mine twenty years ago. Agnes says to fly it again, alone, before I give Tilly my answer.

title: Old Light
tone: Wondering detective story, uneasy and patient
blurb: Light is slow. Sixty-one years ago a settlement called Lantern burned on a moon in Vardh with eleven hundred people in it, and the light of that night is only now reaching systems sixty-one light years out. Dr. Imogen Strand was nine when it happened. She has spent her life building an instrument that can see a settlement from that far, and she has hired you to fly it. Every light year closer, you watch a year later. The record says a reactor failed. Imogen says somebody killed her mother, and someone out there is willing to make the light lie. Misread it, and the people who buried Lantern keep their story. What does the light show that the record does not?
inYourWords: I fly a ship I have paid off and engineered a little, and I keep enough in the bank to get through one bad month. I took Dr. Strand's charter because it paid well and sounded quiet: carry her instrument out into the dark sixty-odd light years from Vardh, keep still, and let it look back. She says that from far enough away, the light of a place is still the place as it was. Sixty-one years ago a settlement called Lantern burned on Vardh 7 a. She was nine, and her mother was in it. She has asked me to take her down to the ice before we start.
beacon: Imogen's array has to be calibrated against a light source that has not changed in a million years, and there is only one kind she trusts. She has marked the nearest Guardian beacon on my chart and says the instrument is useless until it has had a data-link scan of one.

title: Clean Bill
blurb: One cheap salvage run: meta-alloys from a Thargoid site, a Guardian beacon on the way for a bonus, and a buyer waiting at the end. That night your ship starts to tick. Something scratches in the cargo rack, frost grows inside your canopy, and the power drains while you sleep. At dawn Hazard Officer Imre Vasko of the Merope port authority calls, calm and kind and exact: a Thargoid growth came aboard with the salvage, and you have one week to find it and burn it out before your ship is impounded. The mind that came aboard at the beacon has studied war for a million years and never fought one, and it is delighted. Run out the week without finding it, and the ship is impounded with you inside it, and whatever has been ticking since the first night finishes the call it started. What is ticking in there?
inYourWords: I fly a working ship with some engineering on it, and I keep enough in the bank to turn down a bad job. I took this one anyway, because it paid three times the going rate: pick up meta-alloys at a Thargoid site, scan a Guardian beacon on the way for a bonus, and deliver both to a research buyer. The alloys are in the hold now. They are cold to the touch through the crate and they make the cargo rack smell like a struck match. The beacon is one jump away. Easy money, the buyer said. I have heard that before.
beacon: The buyer pays a bonus for a beacon data-link log flown in alongside the alloys: Guardian readings and Thargoid metal in the same hold, side by side. So I fly out to the nearest beacon with the cargo still aboard and run the data-link.

title: The Wishing Run
tone: Urgent race against the clock, warm and brisk
blurb: You spent your last credits on a berth aboard the Wishing Run, a cheap carrier tour to a Guardian beacon where the custom is to speak a wish into the data-link. With the whole tour listening, you wished you knew what you were doing, and they laughed. The next morning a woman's voice came over the tour's channel. She calls herself the Instructor, she has three days to teach you, and she is never wrong about where trouble will be. She teaches one lesson at a time, spends her words as if each one cost her something, and asks what you can see, as though she cannot see it herself. Fall behind, and the three days run out on whoever is giving the lessons, and you never learn who she was. Why does she count in hours?
inYourWords: I have a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits, and no idea what I am doing. I spent nearly everything on a berth on the Wishing Run, a carrier tour that parks beside a Guardian beacon so tourists can make a wish. Mine went out on the tour's open channel, and forty pilots heard me wish I knew what I was doing. Somebody laughed until their mic cut out. This morning a voice on that channel called me by my callsign and said she was the Instructor. Three days, she said. I think the beacon heard me.
beacon: The Wishing Run parks beside a Guardian beacon, and the custom is to speak a wish into the data-link while the scan runs. Spacers say it comes true within three days, the way you asked for it and not the way you meant it. I scanned it, and I made my wish.

title: House Rules
tone: Chilling cult drama, wry and close
blurb: You are broke, your Sidewinder is still in yard paint, and the Rookery is the only place at McMahon Dock that will give you a bunk on credit. Brannagh Tull, a retired navy chief, runs it on the Book: forty rules, oddly numbered, recited at breakfast. The rules work. Rookery pilots are fast, disciplined and trusted, and the best courier work goes to them. You have seven days of probation, then you sign the Book or leave. Eleven names hang on a plaque by the hatch, and nobody talks about how they got there. Sign without asking, and Pim Okafor, who has kept every rule for a year, may be the twelfth. Where did the Book come from?
inYourWords: I spent my last credits on fuel to fly a Guardian beacon scan for a university bounty, and the university withdrew the bounty while I was flying home. I came back to Eravate on fumes, with nothing to sell and nowhere to sleep. At McMahon Dock a woman named Brannagh Tull looked at my ship, looked at me, and handed me a bunk chit and a small grey book. She said I had a week. Pim Okafor, in the next bunk, taught me rule one before I had unpacked: a sequence once begun is completed. I like it here. It is the first place in a long time that has told me what to do.
beacon: A university newsfeed posted a bounty for a fresh data-link scan of a Guardian beacon. I spent everything I had on fuel to fly out and scan one. By the time I was back in the bubble, the bounty had been withdrawn.

title: Safety in Numbers
tone: Creeping friendship horror, cosy on the surface
blurb: You are broke and you do not know a soul out here. Then the New Pilots' Fellowship puts you on an intake channel with three other rookies, and pays a small stipend for one thing: answer roll call every night with your callsign and where you are. Bex Calloway makes you laugh, Orrin Vos reads his stipend slip aloud as a joke, and Kit Halloran worries about everyone. For the first time out here, you have friends. A few nights after the class scans a Guardian beacon together, roll call has five answers, and there are four of you. Then Kit stops answering. Trust the wrong voice, and you are the next pilot nobody hears from. Who is the fifth voice?
inYourWords: I have a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits and nobody to talk to. Last week a message came from the New Pilots' Fellowship: an intake channel for new licences, a small weekly stipend, and one rule. Every night at roll call you give your callsign and where you are, so that somebody always knows. There are four of us. Bex Calloway, who talks to me as if we have known each other for years. Orrin Vos, who reads his stipend slip aloud as a joke. Kit Halloran, who worries for all of us. It is the first time out here that anybody has asked where I am.
beacon: The Fellowship's first class exercise is a Guardian beacon: fly out past the edge of the bubble, make a data-link scan, and report it at roll call for a bonus on the stipend. Nobody on the channel knows what it is meant to teach. Bex says we will all fly it together, over the channel, and nobody gets left behind.

title: Dead Reckoning
tone: Bitter family mystery, quiet and tender
blurb: Your father left when you were six and never sent a word. Now he is dead, and Wenna Hale, the probate clerk at George Lucas in Leesti, is holding the one thing he left you: a data chip with your name on its case, in his handwriting. Its index lists ten stops across the bubble, each with a recording, and every recording is addressed to a child called Sparrow. Nobody has ever called you Sparrow. Stop flying it, and the one thing he left you stays a stranger's promise. Who was Sparrow?
inYourWords: I have a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits, and a father I last saw when I was six. Aldo left to fly survey and never sent so much as a message. Last week a probate clerk named Wenna Hale wrote to say he had died at George Lucas in Leesti, that his debts cancel his savings, and that one thing is left for me: a data chip with my name on its case, in his handwriting. She read me its index. Ten stops, ten recordings, and every one of them addressed to someone called Sparrow. I have never been called Sparrow in my life. The chip is waiting for me at the registry, and I have not decided whether I want to hear his voice.
beacon: Wenna says the first entry on the chip has no recording. It is the coordinates of a Guardian beacon and two words: start here. If he could not be bothered to say anything else, I can at least find out why he sent me there first.

title: Two Flags
tone: Yearning slow-burn romance in two navies, dry and warm
blurb: The day you left the Pilots Federation's starter systems, you were broke, so you enlisted in both navies at the first station past the boundary and took both recruitment stipends. Pilots call that being a two-flagger, and neither navy likes it. Every Imperial recruit needs a patron, and House Talmont's desk drew your name: formal, exact, funny when caught off guard, in a uniform a season out of date. Imperial custom says a patron may not court a client until the client holds a title, so you start climbing. The Federal recruiter laughs at your Imperial colours, your patron will not hear a word about your Federal ones, and Senator Ysolde Talmont, who heads the house, has started asking about you. Lose your nerve, and your patron is sent somewhere you can never follow. Why does your patron never take you to the house?
inYourWords: I have a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits and two enlistments, which is two more than most people with a few hundred credits. The navies may not recruit inside the starter systems, so both keep a desk at the first station outside them, and I walked past both on my first day out. The Federal Navy and the Imperial Navy both pay new recruits a stipend, and nothing in either oath says you can only take one. Lieutenant Hollis Brandt at the Federal desk read my Imperial papers, laughed, and signed me anyway. The Imperial desk said I needed a patron of record, and House Talmont drew my name. My patron read me the rules in a voice like a closed door, then asked whether I had eaten. I have been thinking about that question for three days.
beacon: Every new client of House Talmont brings the house a Guardian beacon scan as a first service, for an archive my patron says is the oldest in Achenar. I would fly a lot further than that to be told well done.

title: Windfall
tone: Nervous windfall thriller, slow-burn and wry
blurb: One week last summer, twelve billion credits arrived in your account from a bank that closed a century ago, with no sender, no message and no mission behind them. You bought a fleet carrier, filled a hangar and made your name on the trade runs, all of it earned at a market and none of it in a war. Now an auditor from the Pilots Federation's accounts office calls every month with one more question, and Cassius Morrow, an Imperial indenture broker with very good lawyers, has filed a claim that the money came out of a salvage he owns. Every answer you find makes the money look worse, and Morrow is less interested in the money than he should be. Get it wrong, and Morrow gets what he is really after, and whoever trusted you with the money pays for it. Who sent you twelve billion credits, and what did they buy?
inYourWords: At the start of the year I had a hauler and a few hundred thousand credits. I worked out where palladium was cheap and where it was not, and I did not stop. Then one week in summer twelve billion credits landed in my account from the Barnard's Star Savings House, which closed a hundred years ago, with nothing attached but a reference number. I checked it three times, and then I bought a fleet carrier, because that is what you do. Now I have a carrier, a hangar of ships and a name made at the market, not in a war. I never asked where the money came from. That was a choice, and I made it quickly. Cassius Morrow has filed a claim to every credit of it, and the Pilots Federation has opened a file. I have been asked to explain myself, and I cannot.
beacon: Morrow's claim says the money came out of a salvage he made beside a Guardian beacon, and it does not say which beacon, which is an odd thing for a lawyer to leave out. Before I answer a word of it, I am going to fly out to one and look for myself.

title: Escort Fee
blurb: A man called Garrick Brand paid you a week's wages to fly him out to a Guardian beacon, watched the scan from your jump seat without a word, and walked off your ship at the next station. He left a sealed courier case in your cabin, with three days on its timer and your pilot licence number etched on the lid. Within the hour, bounty hunters are asking after your ship at every station in the region, and the case will not open. Get it wrong, and a woman you have never met is sentenced when the timer runs out. Why is your licence number on a case you have never seen?
inYourWords: I fly a stock Sidewinder and I have a few hundred credits to my name. Yesterday a man called Garrick Brand paid me a week's wages to take him out to a Guardian beacon and run the scan while he watched. He asked to see my licence before he boarded, sat in my cabin with the door shut all the way home, and left at the next station without saying goodbye. He left a case behind. It has my licence number on the lid, a timer counting down, and it will not open. Now people are asking for me by name.
beacon: A man on the dock paid me a week's wages to fly him out to a Guardian beacon and scan it while he watched. I needed the fare, so I did not ask why.

title: Beginner's Luck
blurb: On a dare made in a starport bar, you flew out and scanned a Guardian beacon, and since you came home good fortune has followed your Sidewinder everywhere it goes, though never into it. A dock hand finds the ring she lost a year ago. The pilot in the next bay is pardoned. Then Ottilie Faraday, the gambler who lost the dare, comes up your boarding ramp and confesses: she paid for all of it, to sell you a luck charm, and she would like half of whatever you earn for three days. Throw her off the ship, and Ottilie, who has never once been lucky, goes back to the life she had, alone. If she paid for the luck, why does it keep happening after her money runs out?
inYourWords: I spent nine years scrubbing hull plate at a starport before I took the Pilots Federation's free Sidewinder, and I have a few hundred credits to my name. A few nights ago, in a starport bar, a gambler called Ottilie Faraday bet me a bottle of something green that I would never fly a stock Sidewinder out to a Guardian beacon and scan it. I did, and last night she paid up. This morning good things started happening to the people around me. None of them have happened to me.
beacon: A gambler in a starport bar bet me a bottle of something green that I would never fly a stock Sidewinder out to a Guardian beacon and scan it. I did it to win the bottle.

title: Night Shift
blurb: You took a week of night-shift supply runs at a small outpost to pay for fuel. On the first night the lights dimmed on a schedule nobody set, the cargo lift ran up and down with nothing in it, and the shift log showed twelve names for eleven workers. The twelfth is yours, logged the day before you arrived. Foreman Dace Mbatha says it is a software fault and to keep working. Luz Arriaga, who has slept on the dorm deck for eleven years, says the station has always done this. The voice that came aboard your ship at the beacon says something in the walls is counting the sleepers, every night, one by one. Get it wrong, and the eleven people on the night shift do not wake up. Who logged you onto the shift before you arrived?
inYourWords: I was a night porter on a passenger liner for eight years. When the liner was retired I took the Pilots Federation's free Sidewinder instead of another liner, because I have been awake while other people sleep for most of my life and I meant to see somewhere while I did it. I have a few hundred credits and nobody waiting for me. A maintenance board at a small outpost listed a fee for a fresh Guardian beacon reading, and I took it. The fee paid for the trip and not much more. The foreman, Dace Mbatha, is short of pilots for the night shift and offered me a week of supply runs. Luz Arriaga, who works the cargo lift, showed me where to sign in. My name was already there.
beacon: A maintenance board at a small outpost listed a fee for a fresh data-link reading of a Guardian beacon, to calibrate its sensors. I accepted it from the board the day before I flew out, scanned one, and brought the reading back.

title: Both Ways
blurb: Your first job for the Kittiwake Cooperative is two contracts for the same sealed crate. Orla Venn's outpost orders it flown to Silas Hask's, and Hask's orders it flown straight back. Both are urgent, both pay, and the two outposts have not spoken to each other in eleven years. Dispatcher Faye Arkwright, three weeks into the job, says to pick one and ignore the other. You do not know any better, so you fly both, back and forth, and before long both outposts are complaining about you, a water company's ship is following you, and the cooperative has ordered the crate taken off you. Get it wrong, and the two outposts finally meet, armed, over a crate you are carrying. Why does each of them keep sending it to the other?
inYourWords: I cooked for six years on an ore barge, and when the barge went to the breakers I took the Pilots Federation's free Sidewinder and a few hundred credits. The Kittiwake Cooperative hires new couriers if they fly out to a Guardian beacon and bring back a reading, because it shows whether a pilot finishes what they start. I spent most of what I had on fuel, brought the reading home, and was hired. Faye Arkwright, the dispatcher, has given me my first job. I have never flown a contract in my life.
beacon: The Kittiwake Cooperative pays new couriers a bonus for a Guardian beacon reading, as a test of whether a pilot finishes what they start. I flew out, scanned one, brought the reading home and was hired.

title: Second Opinion
blurb: You flew a retired doctor, Beatrix Lund, out to a Guardian beacon so she could see one once more before she died, and the two of you scanned it together. Since that morning a young pilot keeps breaking in on your comms: frightened, lost, and sure it is fifty years ago. She calls herself Bea, she is about to make mistakes you can hear coming, and she will listen to nobody but you. Three systems away, Beatrix plays the recordings you send her and goes very quiet. Tell Bea the wrong thing, and an old woman's life comes apart. Who is the frightened pilot who will only listen to you?
inYourWords: My aunt raised me on a tug that hauled ore barges between two moons, and when she sold it she gave me half: enough for a licence, a stock Sidewinder and a few hundred credits. Last week an old woman at the passenger desk asked whether anyone would fly her out to a Guardian beacon. She was Beatrix Lund, a retired doctor, and she said she would like to see one once more before she died. Nobody else would take her in a Sidewinder. She paid me four hundred credits, which doubled what I had, and she did not say a word all the way there.
beacon: A retired doctor, Beatrix Lund, paid me to fly her out to a Guardian beacon so she could see one once more before she died. She asked me to run the data-link scan while she watched, and then I flew her back.

title: The Ninth Life
tone: Scrappy hero story, bright and stubborn
blurb: You drove a pirate wing off a mining camp in a stock Sidewinder, mostly by flying straight at them, and by morning the Ringside newsfeed had named you the Cat and started counting your lives: every fight the Cat walks away from is one more. Now pirates queue to be the ninth. Roo Delacroix, who edits the feed, could not be happier, and the Cat stories are everywhere, including some about fights you have never had. If the ninth fight goes the wrong way, the camps you fly for are raided for good. Why are pirates queuing up to fight a rookie?
inYourWords: I grew up at the mining camps in the rings, sorting ore on a belt for the co-op. When I got my licence and the free Sidewinder, the camps clubbed together for my first tank of fuel, and now I fly their samples and spares for whatever they can pay, which leaves me a few hundred credits. Last week a pirate wing jumped the camp while I was loading. I did the only thing I could think of, which was fly straight at them, and they broke off. By morning Roo Delacroix at the Ringside had called me the Cat, and the miners have not called me anything else since.
beacon: Every miner at the camps knows one thing about the pirates: they will not follow anyone into a system with a Guardian beacon in it. Nobody knows why. If the next wing comes for me shooting to kill, the nearest beacon is where I run, and while I wait them out I may as well scan it.

title: Company Scrip
blurb: The Halberd Mining Concern signs pilots nobody else will: a contract note for the claim licence and a camp berth, steady ore work, and forty other pilots who pay each other in company scrip. Petra Szabo, who keeps trying to organise the camp, says no pilot has ever cleared a note. Gideon Roe, who runs it, says you will be the first, and the ledger agrees with him: your note is falling faster than any pilot could mine. Then Halberd hears that a Federal inspector is coming, and the camp starts getting tidied. If the inspection passes, forty pilots stay in debt for the rest of their lives. Why is yours the only note that clears?
inYourWords: I worked a refinery floor for six years, until the refinery shut. The severance bought a stock Sidewinder and a few hundred credits of fuel, and nobody was hiring a pilot with no hours. Halberd was. They do not take your credits; they count your tons. Every ton I refine and sell is logged against my contract note, for the claim licence, the berth and the training, and when the note reaches zero I am a free pilot with a camp full of friends. Gideon Roe, who runs the camp, shook my hand as if he meant it. Petra Szabo, who has spent months trying to organise it, told me to read the note twice and keep every receipt. I read it once and signed.
beacon: Halberd's contract makes every new pilot fly a safety survey before they get claim work: a data-link scan of the nearest Guardian beacon. Gideon says it calibrates the survey kit. Petra says it is to see whether a new pilot will make a long unpaid trip because the company told them to. It is in the contract either way, so I am going.

title: The Tenant
blurb: A Sidewinder has no room to hide anything, and something is living in yours. The cockpit is warm when it should be cold, a second life-support readout you never fitted is counting down on your comms panel, and when the canopy shuts there is breathing on the comms. Dock inspector Sully Marchetti listens once, goes pale, and offers to buy the ship for parts that same afternoon. The core you brought back from the beacon has swept all three compartments for a boarder, found none, and only grown keener. The readout keeps counting, and the breathing goes quiet whenever you speak. Let it reach zero, and whatever is breathing in there stops for good. What is breathing in a ship with nowhere to hide?
inYourWords: I ran the night shift on the water reclamation plant at Beagle 2 Landing for eleven years, and the only cockpit I ever sat in was a simulator in the station school. Then my ticket came up in the station's ship lottery, the one the refit yard on the lower ring pays for every quarter: one recovered Sidewinder, refitted, licence fees paid, for a resident with no ship. My mother cried at the draw. Now I have the ship, a licence a week old and a few hundred credits. The lottery has a custom older than the yard: a winner's first flight is out to a Guardian beacon and back, for luck, and my mother made me promise. I flew it two days ago and scanned the beacon. Since then the cockpit has been warm at night, there is a second life-support readout on my comms panel that I never fitted, and when I shut the canopy something on the comms is breathing. Sully Marchetti, the dock inspector, listened to it once and offered to buy my ship for parts.
beacon: The lottery at Beagle 2 Landing has a custom older than the yard that pays for it: a winner's first flight is out to a Guardian beacon and back, for luck. My mother made me promise, so I flew out in my lottery Sidewinder and scanned it two days ago.

title: Odd Couple
blurb: A pilot called Wren, whom you never met, has died and left you half of a standing medicine contract. The other half belongs to Ezra Quill, a fussy retired accountant who has not left his station in twenty years, and the contract pays only when both of you fly every run in the same ship. Ezra is space-sick by the second jump, hates your music and corrects every docking. The run goes to Lowmeadow, a farming settlement that has lived under blockade for twenty years, and every month the pickets sit a little closer to the drop. Fail, and Lowmeadow goes without medicine, and Ezra goes back to his station for good. Why would Wren split one contract between two people who had never met?
inYourWords: I have a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits, and until last week no prospects at all. Then a registry clerk called Orla Fenwick sent for me. A pilot called Wren had died, and his will left me half of a standing contract: medicine, flown out to a farming settlement called Lowmeadow, past a blockade. I never met Wren. I do not know why he picked me. The other half went to Ezra Quill, a retired accountant who read every clause twice while I signed, and the contract pays only if we both fly every run, in the same ship. Ezra has brought a cushion, a sick bag and a list of my docking faults. We leave tomorrow.
beacon: Ezra says a museum pays for data-link readings of Guardian beacons, and he insisted we take one on the way out. He has a debt he will not explain. I needed the fuel money anyway.

title: The Inspector's Year
tone: Bitter apprenticeship drama, dry and tender
blurb: You are broke, and the only paid apprenticeship on the board is a year as pilot and assistant to Mags Dunleavy, the Pilots Federation flight-safety inspector every dock in the bubble loves to hate. She grounds ships for faults other inspectors shrug at, and years ago she grounded your mother's. You have told nobody that. Every case she hands you makes that old grounding harder to call a mistake, and a pilot she grounded last year is gathering names against her. Look away when it counts, and a ship full of passengers leaves a dock it should never leave. What really happened to your mother's ship?
inYourWords: I have a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits and one reason to be out here. When I was nine, an inspector named Mags Dunleavy grounded my mother's passenger ship, the Kittiwake, for a crack the yard swore was a shadow on the scan. My mother lost her run. Three weeks later she died flying a borrowed cargo ship to pay for a second opinion. Joss Kettering, who flew wing with her for twenty years and has been Uncle Joss to me all my life, says the grounding killed her. Now Dunleavy needs an apprentice for a year, and nobody else applied. She has not asked about my family, and I have not told her.
beacon: Dunleavy starts every inspection year at the same Guardian beacon. She has it scanned to check her instruments against the one thing out here that never changes, and this year her apprentice flies her there and makes the scan.

title: The Finder
blurb: You had flown your Sidewinder for a month when you made your first find: a pilot's ship lost nine years ago, sitting in plain sight near a Guardian beacon where nobody had thought to look. Then you found another, and another. The search-and-rescue coordinator at Ebbrells Watch, who has no time for heroes, starts sending you the names nobody else will look for, the coordinator's own parents among them, and the newsfeeds start calling you the Finder. Verity Ondo, who pays for every search the Watch flies, thanks you warmly and asks you to rest. Stop looking, and more families on the frontier never learn what happened to the pilots they lost. Why do the lost ships keep turning up where nobody looked?
inYourWords: I spent six years at the lost property desk of a busy starport, finding things for people who had given up on them. I was good at it, and I was bored. So I took the Pilots Federation's free Sidewinder and flew it out to the frontier, past the Synuefe colonies, with a few hundred credits and a habit of looking where nobody else does. The only work out here that pays a pilot like me is at Ebbrells Watch, where the search-and-rescue coordinator keeps a board of pilots nobody ever found, and has no time for anyone who calls themselves a hero.
beacon: The search-and-rescue post at Ebbrells Watch pays a few hundred credits to any pilot who flies out to a Guardian beacon and makes a data-link scan, because the beacons log the ships that pass them and lost pilots sometimes steer for them. It is the lowest-paid job on the board. The coordinator told me not to bother. I took it.

title: Apprentice Wings
blurb: Emrys Ash is selling his flight school at the end of the season, and you are the only student it has left. You have three months of lessons to go, a checkride at the end of each one, and a teacher who turns up late, calls you by the wrong name and lies about where he goes on his rest days. Junia Penrose in docking control says he was the best racer in the sector until the crash, and that nobody asks him about it. Then the buyer starts asking about him too. Fail your wings, and the school closes with its last student unqualified, and the last line in Emrys Ash's record is a failure. Who is Emrys really teaching?
inYourWords: I have a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits and half a set of wings. The passenger lines will not take a pilot without school wings, so I spent my savings on six months at the cheapest flight school in the sector, which is Emrys Ash's. Now I know why it was cheap. He is late to every lesson, he calls me Oren, and I have told him my name eleven times. Junia Penrose, who runs docking control at the outpost where he keeps his hangar, says to let him. Three months in, he told me he is selling the school at the end of the season, and that he will not sign another page of my logbook until I have flown out to a Guardian beacon and scanned it.
beacon: Emrys says every student of his flies out to a Guardian beacon and scans it before he signs anything, so that they have seen something older than themselves. He says it has always been the first lesson. He forgot to tell me for three months.

title: Same Name
blurb: You came to Jasmine's Rest, a farming outpost in Alrai Sector NC-V b2-4, with a cheap delivery and no reputation at all. By the time your ship was on the pad, the whole store knew your name. A pilot with that name took the outpost's harvest money a month ago for a delivery that never came, and the registry says the pilot was you. Gwen Abara, who keeps the store, gives you a month to deliver or repay, and the outpost is angry in a way that sounds practised. Every stop on the charter's route remembers you, and somebody very polite has started asking where you go next. Fail, and the outpost's harvest money is gone for good, and your name stays on a debt you never ran up. Who has been flying under your name, and what did they deliver?
inYourWords: For fourteen years I took down the record at a magistrate's court on a station: every word, every date, other people's worst days in order. Then the court bought a machine that does it faster, and I took the Pilots Federation's free Sidewinder instead of a pension. I have a few hundred credits and a licence five weeks old with nothing on it. Nobody out here knows my name, which was rather the point. Then I docked at Jasmine's Rest with a cheap delivery, and Gwen Abara called me by it before I had my helmet off.
beacon: Gwen's clerk, Nell Cassidy, keeps the outpost's records, and the founding charter of Jasmine's Rest has a dispute in it older than anyone living there: two families' water rights pass on only while the old Guardian lights still answer. Nobody has checked in a century. Any Guardian beacon will settle it, Nell says, and the nearest is a long way past the edge of the bubble. Gwen says she will take two thousand off the debt if I fly out, make a data-link scan and bring back the record.

title: The Grand Tour
tone: Sunny sightseeing quest, wry and warm
blurb: Clemency Arden has left her whole estate to whoever finishes her Grand Tour: eight famous sights across the bubble, each scanned from the cockpit in its own window of a six-month calendar, so no ship, however fast, can finish early. Her solicitor, Aurelio Quist, is delighted when you enter in a stock Sidewinder. Two professional explorers, Juno Penrose and Marek Tallis, enter the same day in far better ships, and race each other as if nothing else in the galaxy matters, the prize included. If the wrong entrant finishes, a colony is split in two, and half of it is written out of existence. Why do Juno and Marek hate each other more than they care about winning?
inYourWords: I grew up on an agricultural world under a cloud deck that never once cleared, and I was nineteen before I saw a single star. I left the farm with a stock Sidewinder and a few hundred credits, and I have been staring out of the canopy ever since. In my first week at Fort Harrison in Arcturus a notice went up on the station board. A solicitor called Aurelio Quist was reading out a will: Clemency Arden's estate goes to whoever finishes her Grand Tour, eight famous sights across the bubble, and any pilot may enter. I have never won anything in my life. I entered.
beacon: The first sight on Clemency Arden's list is a Guardian beacon, logged with a data-link scan. Mr Quist says the tour starts with the oldest thing on it, and that my six months start the day I scan it.

title: Lights On
blurb: The outpost is a refuelling stop at the far end of a long route, with one keeper, Anja Roos, a board full of short-haul work and one rule: every ship docked overnight keeps its running lights on. The freighter in the next bay ignored it. By morning its hull was stripped to the frame and its pilot was gone, and Anja says it was raiders. The next night something moves along your own hull, slowly, panel by panel, and stops where your lights are brightest. Get it wrong, and the next pilot who docks without a warning is stripped with their ship. What strips a ship in the dark, and why does Anja know the rule?
inYourWords: I fly relief contracts. When a remote outpost loses its regular hauler for a few days, to a refit or a sick pilot, I cover the board until they are back, then I leave. It pays steady, and nobody asks me to stay. I have a ship I have engineered a little at a time, savings enough for a bad month, and one habit I never break: I sleep aboard, never in a station bunk. My sister says I live like a hermit crab. This contract is three days, at an outpost so far off the lanes that the route sheet calls it the end of the line.
beacon: The route out passed a Guardian beacon, and I had always meant to scan one. I dropped in on the way, held the data-link steady and watched it light.

title: Wrong Cargo
blurb: Sabine Aurel pays well for a fresh Guardian beacon reading, as long as the pilot who brings it home also carries one of her sealed pods and never looks inside. You flew out, ran the scan and turned for home with her pod in your hold, and at the first station it started knocking. Sabine says it is machine parts and the noise is thermal. The contract forbids opening the pod on a penalty larger than everything you have saved, two system authority ships have asked to inspect your hold, and the knocking now has a rhythm. You have three days to delivery. Get it wrong, and whatever is knocking dies in that pod. What is knocking in a sealed pod?
inYourWords: I mine for a living: a working ship with some engineering on it, a few good claims, and enough put by that a bad month does not frighten me. This quarter the rocks ran thin. Sabine Aurel collects Guardian beacon readings, and she paid me better than a month at the belts to fly out to one, scan it and bring the reading home with one of her sealed pods in my hold. I have never carried sealed cargo before, and I read the penalty clause twice before I signed. Since the scan there has been a new voice in my ship. Since the first station, the pod has been knocking.
beacon: Sabine Aurel collects Guardian beacon readings. She paid me better than a month at the belts to fly out to one, run the data-link scan and bring the reading home along with a sealed pod from her warehouse. The rocks had run thin, so I took it.

title: The Expert
blurb: A newsfeed read one footnote in one xenology paper and decided you are the leading authority on Guardian beacons in human space. You haul freight. By the next morning Provost Dorian Kask has booked you to give the keynote at the Zaonce Xenology Colloquium, at Ridley Scott, for a fee you could not earn in ten years, and the hall has sold out. Then Professor Nadia Orme writes. She has studied the beacons for thirty years and been ignored for every one of them, and she asks to share your stage and to tutor you first. You have five days, and four hundred real xenologists will be in the seats. Stumble, and Orme's life's work is laughed off the stage for good. Why does the real expert need a fraud beside her?
inYourWords: I left school at fourteen and have hauled freight ever since. My ship is paid for, the thrusters are engineered, and I have a little put by, which is more than most people I grew up with can say. A week ago I was running cargo past the edge of the bubble, short of fuel money, and a university survey board was paying a few hundred credits for any Guardian beacon log. So I flew to a beacon and pressed the scanner button. Somebody put my log in a footnote. This morning a newsfeed called me the leading expert on Guardian beacons. I have never read a paper in my life. Everything I know about beacons, I learned pressing that button.
beacon: A university survey board was paying for Guardian beacon logs, and I needed fuel money. The scan earned me a footnote in a xenology paper. The story opens a week later, when a newsfeed turns the footnote into a headline.

title: Seven Days Again
blurb: The morning after you scanned a Guardian beacon, everyone you meet is living last week again: the same jokes in the bar, the same complaints on the comms, and the same escort job on the board, the one you turned down. Your own accounts and logs carry on as normal. Only the people repeat. Then Rafe Dunmore, a convoy pilot you know by sight, calls to say that he remembers too, and that the week is his. Somebody Rafe loves dies when this week ends, as they did the last time, and if the week runs the same way it happens again. What does Rafe need you to do differently?
inYourWords: I fly cover for hire: convoys, haulers, anyone with cargo worth stealing. I have a working ship with a few engineers' upgrades in it and enough saved to turn work down. A year ago I lost Joss, who flew my wing for six years. We had made the kind of promise you make at two in the morning: one day we would fly out past the edge of the bubble and scan a Guardian beacon together, just to say we had. Joss never got the chance. So on the anniversary I went alone, and I turned down a good escort job to make the date.
beacon: A year to the day after Joss died, I flew out past the edge of the bubble to keep our promise and made the data-link scan of a Guardian beacon for both of us. I turned down a good escort job to be there on the day.

title: Successor
blurb: For forty years, when a distress call goes out on the frontier stations, one name answers it: Longwatch. Now Teodor Vashti, the old pilot behind the name, has picked you to carry it after him, and he has six months to teach you everything he knows: the patrols, the rescues, the newsfeeds. The stations love the handover, and the newsfeeds love it more. Then Juniper Tess, who flew on his wing for twenty years, warns you that Teodor never chose a successor before because he never meant to stop. Get it wrong, and the frontier stations lose their protector, and six months of training count for nothing. Why is Teodor really stepping down?
inYourWords: I fly a ship I own outright, engineered a little, and I keep enough put by to ride out one bad month. I owe nobody anything, which out here is rarer than it sounds. Last week Teodor Vashti, who has flown as Longwatch since before I was born, found me in a starport bar. He said he had read the rescue log for the whole frontier and that my name kept turning up on distress calls nobody paid me to answer. Then he asked me to take his name when he retires. I laughed. He did not. He says the training takes six months, and the first lesson is a flight to a Guardian beacon.
beacon: Every year, on the day he first flew as Longwatch, Teodor flies to a Guardian beacon and makes a data-link scan of it. He calls it signing the watch book: the oldest thing out here that still keeps watch, and the one he answers to. This year he has asked me to make the scan for him, and he has not said why.

title: The Volunteer
blurb: The Volunteer Rescue Service answers the calls nobody else will, on no money, out of a rented outpost, by a rule book the size of a hull plate. Captain Una Fairweather takes you on, and within a month the newsfeeds have a name for you and every call in the region asks for you by it. Then Osric Lamb, whose firm Sureline Recovery rescues anyone who can pay, offers to buy the Service, and Fairweather drops the offer in the recycler unopened. The money runs out at the end of the month, and with it the only rescue cover the poorest systems in the region have. Why will she not even read it?
inYourWords: I run fast freight: small, urgent and paid by the hour, in a ship I have engineered for one thing, which is getting there first. Ten years of it have left me a decent account and no particular reason to stop. Last month I was the nearest ship to a distress call, and I heard the Volunteer Rescue Service's only pilot on watch say she was forty minutes out. I got there in six. Captain Una Fairweather sent me a message the next morning, three words long: report for induction.
beacon: Every new Volunteer flies to a Guardian beacon and scans it before their first watch. Captain Fairweather says it is the oldest custom in the Service and nobody remembers how it started. The rule book says only that it is to be done, and done properly.

title: Bounty on Myself
blurb: Every bounty board in the region carries your ship's name: a large, legal posting from the Ostrander Compact, a faction you have never flown for, for an attack on a Compact ship on a date twelve days from now. You have not done it. You have not done anything yet. Hunters who read the board start dropping out of supercruise behind you, the Compact will not hear an appeal until the day after the date, and the core you brought back from a Guardian beacon trusts nobody, least of all you. Kasimir Reyes, a hunter with good manners, offers to keep you alive for half your savings, paid when it is over. Get it wrong, and the attack the posting names happens anyway, and the whole region remembers it as yours. Why does the bounty name a crime that has not happened yet?
inYourWords: I haul freight in a ship I have engineered as far as I can afford, and I keep savings enough for a bad month. Two years ago I co-signed a loan for Dario Venn, who flew on my wing, and Dario took the money and disappeared. The lender says the debt is mine now and sent a collector, Ottilie Brack, to get it. I do not think I owe it, and I am not handing her my savings to find out. So for a month I have been hiding in the one kind of system nobody looks in: an empty one with nothing in it but a Guardian beacon. Two days ago I scanned the beacon to pass the time, and something came aboard with the data that has not stopped talking since. The same day my ship's name went up on every bounty board in the region, for an attack I have not made, on a date that has not come. Ottilie Brack stopped calling three weeks before that, and I took it for luck.
beacon: I was hiding from a debt collector in a system with nothing in it but a Guardian beacon, because nobody looks there. With nothing else to do, I flew in close and scanned the beacon. That was two days before the story opens.

title: The Fourth Witness
blurb: On the night you scanned the Guardian beacon in Synuefe QA-E b45-4, two ships collided there and a hauler pilot named Harl Duveen died. Three witnesses saw it and no two of them agree. The fourth record is yours: the traffic log puts your transponder in the system at the minute of the collision, when your docking log, and your own memory, put you asleep a jump away at Sternberg Platform. Tribunal Clerk Oriel Mace has given you until the hearing to explain your own record, and refuses every request for more time. Fail, and Juno Pritchard, the nineteen-year-old courier who survived the crash, is convicted of the killing. How was your ship somewhere you were not?
inYourWords: I fly survey contracts for the colony boards out past Synuefe: arrive, scan every body, sell the data, move on. Eleven years of it, a Krait Phantom with a drive an engineer tuned for range, enough savings to turn down a bad contract, and a log without a single fine in it. My first ship was a Cobra Mk III, which I sold to a breaker's yard six years ago, and I have not thought about it since. Yesterday the contract took me to Synuefe QA-E b45-4. I scanned the Guardian beacon there because it was on the list, flew one jump to Sternberg Platform, docked at ten past nine and slept until morning. I remember every minute of it. In the morning a summons from the traffic authority's tribunal at Leonards Legacy was waiting: my transponder was logged in Synuefe QA-E b45-4 at twenty to midnight, the minute two ships struck each other there and a man died. I have the docking log that says I was on a pad a jump away. Tribunal Clerk Oriel Mace says that is exactly what I have to explain.
beacon: My survey contract for Synuefe QA-E b45-4 listed everything in the system worth logging, and the Guardian beacon was on the list. I scanned it with the data-link and flew on to Sternberg Platform for the night. The summons came the next morning.

title: The Eulogy
tone: Bittersweet grief comedy, wry and tender
blurb: Your oldest friend, Fenwick Bly, has died owing favours, apologies and the odd truth across the bubble, though by his ledger not one credit. His will leaves you the ledger and two jobs: settle every debt in it in person, then give his eulogy. His sister, Mags Bly, thinks the eulogy should have been hers. Each stop turns up a Fenwick you never knew, and a few debts that do not add up. Fail, and the people he owed never hear the apology they have waited years for. Whose debts are you really paying?
inYourWords: I have never owed anyone a credit. I fly a working ship I have engineered one piece at a time, I keep some savings, and I pay my docking fees before I land. Fenwick Bly was the opposite. We met crewing a mining ship when I was nineteen and he was already too old for it, and since then he has borrowed money from me forty times and paid me back thirty-nine. Ten years ago, the week after we last flew the lanes together, he practically pushed me onto a long contract out past the edge of the bubble, and I did not see him for two years. Now his heart has given out in a hostel bunk, and his sister Mags Bly has called me to the bar where he drank to hear his will. He has left me his ledger, his ashes and his eulogy.
beacon: Fen's will asks for his ashes to be scattered at a Guardian beacon. He never cared which one: he said they had waited a million years for somebody to say something nice at one. The will says to log it with a data-link scan, so the first entry in his ledger can be marked settled.

title: Repo
blurb: You bought your ship second-hand and paid for it in full. Then a repossession agent met you at the foot of your own ramp with a court order: the previous owner registered a lien on the ship eleven days before he sold it, and nobody told you. Until a magistrate hears the claim in a month, the agent flies with you, sleeps in your spare seat and inventories every panel of your hull. The agent is rude, exact and broke, and so are you. Then a ship starts docking two pads down from yours at every starport, and its captain calls your ship by its old owner's name. Get it wrong, and the agent loses the only licence and the only work left, and whoever is following you reaches your ship first. What did the previous owner leave in your walls?
inYourWords: For nine years I assessed wrecks for a shipping underwriter. I flew out, read what was left, and told the owner what it was worth, which was always less than they hoped. I saved, took my engineering in trade, and last year bought a ship of my own from a broker at a starport who swore it was clean, with enough left over to keep it fuelled for a year. I checked the registry myself. I check everything. It was clean. Then I came back from a run to find a clamp on my landing gear and a repossession agent sitting on my ramp, eating my last ration bar, holding a court order and a lien I had never seen. The agent spent the first hour telling me what my ship is worth. It is less than I hoped.
beacon: The court wants an inventory of my ship's logs, and the agent is doing it line by line. The previous owner's last logged data-link scan was at a Guardian beacon, and the inventory says the scanner has to be proven original by a fresh handshake with one. Any beacon will do, the agent says, and the agent is not getting out to walk.

title: Off the Record
blurb: Independent pilots are vanishing from the frontier, and a reporter from the Farline newsfeed turns up at your berth with a year's budget, a generous publisher and your signature on thirteen of the losses. The reporter is sharp, secretive and funnier than the work deserves, and every lead brings the two of you closer: to each other, and to a name that keeps turning up at the end of dead pilots' trails, the Ferryman. Then the sources start to go quiet, one after another. Fail, and the pilots go on vanishing, and the one story the reporter has given a whole career to comes to nothing. Where are the missing pilots going?
inYourWords: I assess losses for an underwriter on the frontier. When a ship goes missing out there, I fly out, find what is left of it, and sign the loss, so the policy pays and the debt dies with the pilot. I have a good ship with some engineering done, and enough saved to quit, though I never have. Eleven years of other people's last flights. Nobody waits for me at any station, which suits the work. Then a reporter from the Farline sat down across from me with thirteen of my sign-offs and asked me, very politely, why none of them had a body.
