beacon: The reporter has heard that somebody leaves messages for the missing in the data of a Guardian beacon, and asks you to fly out and scan one for the story.

title: Standing Debt
tone: Dusty civic drama, dry and wry
blurb: Every quarter Hadid City draws one registered pilot by lot for the seventh seat on its Harbour Board, and this quarter it drew you: three months of berthing fees, dockyard business and very old people being polite. Constance Abara has chaired the board for thirty years and hopes you enjoy your quarter. Then you read the ledgers. Every month for a hundred years, the estate of a dead man has paid the same debt, and the debt has never fallen by a credit. Each time you ask, the board moves on to the next item, the old minutes go missing, and the crews in Femi Adair's dockyard stop talking when you walk in. Let it go, and those crews go on paying, every month, for a board that answers to nobody. Who has been paying a dead man's debt for a hundred years?
inYourWords: I have a working ship, some engineering done on it and savings enough for a bad month, and I keep a berth at Hadid City in LTT 1873 because it is cheap and I am never there. Two years ago I limped in after a fight with half my hull gone, and Femi Adair's yard crews rebuilt my ship for less than it was worth. I have kept the berth since. Every pilot registered at Hadid City goes into the quarterly lottery for the Harbour Board, and nobody I know has ever been drawn. Now I have. Three months, a seat at a long table, and a stack of ledgers older than anyone sitting at it. Constance Abara, the chair, shook my hand and told me nobody expects a lottery member to read them.
beacon: The board's bylaws say every new member scans a Guardian beacon within their first month, under a rule the founder wrote into the charter a hundred years ago. Nobody on the board can tell me why, and not one of them has ever skipped it. Ambrose Tenney, the clerk, has found me the nearest one.

title: The Meridian
blurb: Thirty years ago the expedition ship Meridian came home from its last survey, and its crew took its drive apart: twelve of them, one part each, carried off to twelve homes across the bubble. Its captain, Odette Achterberg, is eighty-one, and she has asked you to spend a year flying the bubble to bring every part back to Lavoisier Dock, one crew member at a time. Some of them will not answer her messages. Benedikt Sorel, who collects famous ships, has offered her a fortune for the Meridian as it lies, and at the end of the year the dock clears its berth whether the ship can fly or not. Fail, and the Meridian goes to Sorel in pieces, and the twelve people who flew it never stand in the same room again. Why did a crew take their own ship apart?
inYourWords: I fly spares. Drive coils, power couplings, a sensor housing somebody needs by the end of the week: if a workshop in the bubble is short of a part, I am usually the one who brings it. My ship is fitted for the work and paid for, and I have a little put by. That is how Odette Achterberg found me. She is eighty-one, she captained an expedition ship called the Meridian for forty years, and she has not flown since it was laid up at Lavoisier Dock in Riedquat. She does not need a part found. She needs twelve of them, and she knows exactly where each one is, because she knows exactly who took it. She has offered me a year's pay to go and ask for them. She has not said why her crew took them, and I have not asked yet.
beacon: Before anything else, Odette asked me to scan a Guardian beacon, because the Meridian made the same scan on the first day of its last expedition. She would like her parts collected by a pilot who has seen what her crew saw that day. It is an odd thing to ask of a courier, and I went.

title: The Lost Fleet
blurb: Three hundred years ago the Ninefold Convoy left the bubble with nine ships and a fortune in rare metals, and was never seen again. Now the Lisle Salvage Consortium has bought a fragment of its log, and Emory Kerr, its expedition lead, reads the bearings aloud to three hired pilots: you, Edda Malloy, who has forty years in salvage and no patience for Kerr, and Remy Okonjo, who is cheerful about everything. Every stop on the route turns up a convoy wreck. The trouble is the count. Nine ships left, the wrecks are past a dozen and still coming, and two expeditions have flown this route before you and never come back. Then a stripping outfit starts turning up a day behind you. Fail, and the breakers take everything the convoy left behind, and Kerr loses what he has staked on this route. Why are there more wrecks than there were ships?
inYourWords: I have a ship with a good jump range, some engineering done on it and savings that last about two months between jobs. I fly salvage: crashed ships, lost cargo, and black boxes for families who need to know what happened. I like finding what other people have lost track of. When the Lisle Salvage Consortium asked for pilots to fly with Emory Kerr after the Ninefold Convoy, I signed before I had finished reading. Kerr is charming, late to everything, and paid by the wreck. Edda Malloy, who flies the second ship, says that is all you need to know about him. Remy Okonjo, who flies the third, says she is too hard on him. I have not decided.
beacon: The Ninefold Convoy's log fragment begins with a navigation fix taken beside a Guardian beacon. Kerr sends each of us out to data-link scan a beacon, so that all three of us start the hunt from the same place.

title: Open Day
blurb: Harbourmaster Teodora Quist has had enough of fleet carriers crowding her system, and the carrier owners have one chance to keep their berths: a three-day open day aboard your carrier, beside a Guardian beacon, for anyone who wants to come. Two thousand visitors have booked, along with a school trip, a protest group with banners and the celebrity chef Marius Bellweather, who is cooking the buffet. You have commanded fleets in three wars. You have never run anything with a buffet. By the first evening the cold store has failed, the landing pads are double-booked and the sprinklers have gone off over the concourse, and Quist is counting incidents. If she cancels the open day, every carrier crew in the system loses its berth. Who keeps sabotaging the open day?
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of engineered ships and more credits than I will ever spend. I have flown lead in three wars, and I have never once been asked to organise a party. The carrier owners in this system met to decide who would host the open day Harbourmaster Teodora Quist asked for. I missed the meeting, so they chose me. I have booked Marius Bellweather to cook, because everyone said a famous name would bring the crowds, and I have read his rider twice without understanding most of it. The visitors arrive this morning.
beacon: Every open day needs something to look at, and the best thing in this system is the Guardian beacon. I jumped my carrier in beside it and ran the data-link scan myself the night before the visitors came, so that it would be lit when they arrived.

title: Nobody Knows You
blurb: The morning after the last beacon scan of a long expedition, nobody knows your face. Your carrier crew are polite to a stranger, the friends you came home to ask your name, and Osei Marr, who has run your deck for nine years, asks to see your authorisation. Your ships, your credits and your carrier are all still yours, and your ship still knows you. Only Hattie Lune, the dock cook who shared the beacon reading with you, remembers who you are. She says it will pass in three days, and she does not seem surprised. Come out of the three days the wrong way, and a woman nobody remembers stays unknown for the rest of her life. Why does nobody know you, and why does Hattie?
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of engineered ships and more credits than I will ever spend. For eight months I have been out past the edge of the bubble with thirty crew, charting systems nobody had named, and Osei Marr has kept the carrier's deck running the whole way, as he has for nine years. On the way home we restocked at a dock outpost on the fringe, and the cook there, Hattie Lune, fed my crew for a week, told the best stories the galley has heard, and asked me more about Guardian beacons than any cook should. When she heard where we were stopping next, she asked to come along.
beacon: The last stop of the expedition was a Guardian beacon. Hattie asked to fly out to it with me in a hangar ship and share the data-link reading, because she had never seen one lit. I said yes, and we ran the scan together. That was last night.
